# Design exploration

A design exploration is a dialog. **The user is the designer. You find and frame. The user
chooses.** A finding is not a licence to pick the fix.

The unit of work is one open question, with every answer drawn side by side at the same
geometry: a **sketch** on a product, or a **call** in a repository with the old setup. A variant wins
or loses only against the other variants of its question.

## The rules

1. **One open call at a time.** Take one question. Draw its variants. Stop.
2. **Put the variants in the call, then name your pick.** Two to four variants, drawn for
   real, side by side, labelled, with what each one costs. Your pick is a proposal. Never ask
   a yes/no question about content, and never ask the user what they want: deliver strong
   variants, and the user picks.
3. **Commit only when the user says commit.** A merge the user makes in Ethlete Studio counts as
   that word for the merged part: commit the part, not the open sketches.
4. **A clear rejection starts the next call.** Settle and record the rejected call, then draw
   the next focused question automatically, within the user's original scope. Stop only when the
   user asks to pause or end the exploration, or when their feedback leaves no grounded next
   question.
5. **Keep the answer short.** 120 words at most.
6. **A reference informs, it is not a template.** Before you show a round led by a reference
   (a Figma file, another product), state the problem the reference solves, the principle you take
   from it, and how each variant differs in concept. Then review the variants beside the reference
   for literal copies. Derive the composition from the product's own visual language; a new palette
   or spacing on the reference's layout is not a different concept.

Confirm the step size once, at the start. Do not ask again at every stop. A task is not
finished while the user is still talking about it.

## What one stop looks like

- The question, in one sentence.
- The sketch (or call slug) to look at.
- The variants, labelled A, B, C, one line each.
- Your pick, one line on why.
- Nothing else. No next step, no second finding.

**Do not send a screenshot.** The user keeps the call open. Screenshot only for your own check that a
variant renders: `et design shot <layer>/<name> --states [--variants]` draws one contact sheet. Every
flag, the motion shots and the raw screenshot script are in `reference-shots.md` (bundled next to this skill). Do not
write a scratch script for batch shots.

If a second defect appears, add it to the open list and give it one line. Do not draw it.

## Where the variants are drawn

The exploration's plan file names the tool. Two shapes exist.

**A repository with a `.ethlete/design` folder** keeps one design system per **product**, and the
user reads and decides in Ethlete Studio. The tool is `et design`, from `@ethlete/cli`; run
`et design --help` for every command, `et design <command> [<subcommand>] --help` for one.
In the SDK checkout, `yarn design` builds the CLI before each call; in a check-and-shot loop,
build once and call `node dist/libs/cli/src/index.js design` instead.

```
.ethlete/design/
  config.json                         the port and one `products` entry each
  <product>/<layer>/<part>/           layer: foundations, components, elements, pages
  <product>/flows/<name>.json         a flow: pages and their states joined by lines
  <product>/sketches/<layer>-<name>/  an open sketch: sketch.json and one folder per variant
  <product>/comments/<id>.json        a comment the user wrote in Studio
  calls/                              old calls: Legacy, read-only
```

Studio no longer takes new calls. **New work goes to a product, never to a new call**; do not run
`et design new`. Old calls stay in Studio's Legacy tab as reference for moving them into a
product. They take no picks and no new variants.

## Hard rules for products and sketches

- A change to a merged part, also a small one, is a **sketch**; never edit a merged part directly. When
  nothing is to choose, the sketch has one variant (`--variants a`). Variants are alternatives, never a state
  of another variant. Two to four variants, each with its cost; run `sketch check` before `sketch ready`.
- **Never run `sketch merge` or `sketch discard`, and never pick a variant.** Studio merges on the user's
  click. After a pick or discard, do not merge. Run `sketch reject` or `reopen` only when the user did.
- Mark a sketch `ready` only when no change to it waits on anything; otherwise `sketch hold`.
- Every write command takes `--by <model id>`. **Never guess your id**: use the one your prompt names, or ask
  the coordinator or the user before you write.
- Run `et design accept` only after the user approved a direct edit. Remove a part only with
  `et design part remove`, never `git rm`.
- Studio takes no new calls: never run `et design new`. New work goes to a product.
- Share code between variants in the sketch's `shared/` folder only; no shared parameter or branch for one
  variant. An asset is one file in `<product>/assets/`, never inlined.
- A user comment to combine variants is a new variant in a new round (`sketch variant --from --round --note`).
- Read the inbox at the start of a session and after each `ready`. Answer with `inbox done <id> --note`,
  ask with `comment reply --question` only when you cannot go on. Only the user resolves a thread.
- Use the `ethlete-design` MCP tools when they are in your tool list, and call `sketch_report` before every
  variant edit.
- Draw from the design system, never invent a button or field: the product's parts, then SDK components via
  `ng()`, then new. Colours come from the SDK theming systems, never your own tokens. A part exists only
  because the user picked a sketch.
- A wireframe is rough and fast: regions and names only, no polish, no subagent, one sketch per screen.
- Do not start a design stage before the one above it is settled: wireframes, foundations, logo and CI,
  components, elements, pages, prototype.

Details, commands and examples, read on demand:

- `reference-products-and-sketches.md` (bundled next to this skill): creating a product, every `sketch` command, shared code,
  assets, rounds, `--by`, the merge and accept flow. Read before the first sketch command.
- `reference-inbox-and-mcp.md` (bundled next to this skill): reading and answering comments, thread states, the MCP tools.
- `reference-flows-and-wireframes.md` (bundled next to this skill): flow JSON, the wireframe kit and its rules.
- `reference-check-and-notes.md` (bundled next to this skill): `design check` rules and warnings, drawing-file constraints,
  `setup`, `ngStates`, notes.
- `reference-order-and-design-system.md` (bundled next to this skill): the stage order, component states and
  `interactionRows`, `ng()` and form fields, theming rules.
- `reference-shots.md` (bundled next to this skill): every `shot` flag, motion shots, the screenshot script.

## Check before you look

A broken build draws an overlay, so a screenshot of it looks like a design. **One check
covers that, and it is the whole gate.** Name the files you changed, never a whole project,
which is far slower and can fight the user's own editor.

With `et design`, run the checker from the checkout it draws:

```bash
et design check --lint <changed files> --tsconfig
```

`--tsconfig` with no path types every call of the checkout. `--tsconfig` also types each variant of
an open sketch and prints the tsc output of a failing one. `--checkout <path>` names another
one.

With a Storybook, copy `check-story.mjs` (bundled next to this skill) to the **repository root** first:

```bash
node check-story.mjs --lint <changed files> --tsconfig apps/<app>/.storybook/tsconfig.json
```

Both take about four seconds and need no dev server. Then stop and hand the slug to the
user. Do not also render it in a browser: it costs a browser launch, and both tools
transpile without type checking, so the render reports `ok` on a file that does not
compile. Open it only when the check passes and the drawing still does not appear:

```bash
et design check --call <slug>             # every variant of the call
et design check --call <slug> --variant b # one of them
node check-story.mjs --tsconfig <path> --story <story-id>
```

A passing check says the variant builds, not that it looks good. Before `sketch ready`, look at
each variant at a readable scale and in its whole host page, and critique its hierarchy, spacing,
nesting and host context together. Drop a variant that is technically valid but visually weak
before the user sees it. In your summary, say "renders correctly", never "good" or "approved":
the user decides that.

## Delegating a sketch

Every brief names `model: opus`, and every prompt names the exact model id the sub-agent runs on,
for example "Your model id is `claude-opus-5-5`; pass `--by claude-opus-5-5` to every write
command." You know the id because you chose the model; the sub-agent does not, and must not guess.

1. **One agent per sketch.** It draws all the variants of the sketch. Give it the sketch folder, the
   fixture it must not change, and the claim of each variant. Do not spawn one agent per
   variant: each would re-read the skill, the call, the fixture and the example, about 45-57k
   tokens each, so the cost is several times higher. Calls are independent, so several calls
   can run at once, one agent each.
2. **One check-and-fix agent, after the drawing agents return.** Give it the changed files
   and the call slug. It runs the check above, fixes what it reports, and repeats until the
   check says `ok`. It may not change what a variant draws, only what stops it rendering.
3. **One write-up agent, once the user settles the sketch in Studio.** Give it the verdict in the
   user's own words and the plan file. It records what won, what lost and why, it sets each
   variant's `verdict` in an old call's `call.ts` (a product sketch needs none; the merge sets the note). It runs while you open
   the next call.

## Writing it down

Every settled call goes in the exploration's plan file: what won, what lost, and why. Keep
an **Open** list for the calls not yet made. A rejected variant written down stops the next
session from drawing it again. After a clear rejection, use that record to frame and draw the
next call; do not wait for the user to type “continue”.
